title: The lesson on pronunciation: six things a reciter must get right
theme: Before the Upaniṣad teaches anything about meaning, it names the six aspects of sound that a student must learn to hear and to say.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «शिक्षैव शीक्षा । दैर्घ्यं छान्दसम्» — the long ī is a Vedic lengthening of śikṣā
Śaṅkara: «विस्पष्टम् आ समन्तात्प्रकथयिष्यामः» — set out clearly and fully
Śaṅkara: «वर्णः अकारादिः» — the sounds a and the rest
Śaṅkara: «स्वर उदात्तादिः» — udātta and the other accents
Śaṅkara: «मात्रा ह्रस्वाद्याः» — short, long and the rest
Śaṅkara: «बलं प्रयत्नविशेषः» — a particular effort of articulation
Śaṅkara: «साम वर्णानां मध्यमवृत्त्योच्चारणं समता» — pronouncing the sounds evenly, at a middle pace
Śaṅkara: «सन्तानः सन्ततिः, संहितेत्यर्थः» — the joining of sounds, saṃhitā

words.gram: past passive participle, m. nom. sg.

sandhi.rule: A final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
A final i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). iti + uktaḥ → ity uktaḥ.

morphology.note: The ordinary word is śikṣā, from the desiderative of śak, ‘to wish to be able’, hence ‘learning, training’. The long ī is Vedic (Śaṅkara, Kūranārāyaṇa and Rāmānanda all say so). Madhva’s text and the ordinary spelling read śikṣām.

Future of khyā with the preverbs vi and ā, ‘we shall explain’. Śaṅkara notes that the form comes from cakṣ, for which khyā is substituted: «चक्षिङः ख्याञादिष्टस्य व्याङ्पूर्वस्य व्यक्तवाक्कर्मण एतद्रूपम्». The plural is the teacher’s.
Nominative of the neuter sāman. Here not ‘chant’ (the Sāmaveda) but ‘evenness’: Kūranārāyaṇa derives it from the root of sāntvana, ‘to make even, conciliate’, and glosses «उच्चारणे समता साम».
Past participle of vac, ‘to speak’, agreeing with śīkṣādhyāyaḥ. Its tense looks back: the lesson has been ‘stated’ — in six words.

translation.literal: We shall explain the śikṣā. Letter, accent; measure, effort; evenness, connection. Thus [has been] stated the lesson on śikṣā.
translation.readable: We will now explain the science of pronunciation: the sounds, the accent, the length, the effort, the evenness, the joining. That is the lesson on pronunciation.

anvaya: [वयम्] शीक्षाम् व्याख्यास्यामः । वर्णः स्वरः मात्रा बलम् साम सन्तानः [इति शीक्षायाः विषयाः] । इति शीक्षाध्यायः उक्तः ॥
syntax: A heading, a list and a closing formula. The heading is a promise in the future tense with the teacher’s plural, ‘we shall explain’. The list is six nouns in the nominative with no verb, set two to a line. The closing ‘thus has been stated the lesson on śikṣā’ uses the past participle as a predicate: the whole lesson is the list.

ambiguities.topic: Is this the lesson, or only its table of contents?
ambiguities.note: The text says the lesson ‘has been stated’, yet it states only six headings. Kūranārāyaṇa draws the consequence: the details belong to the science of śikṣā, and here they are only recalled «तत्सर्वं शिक्षाशास्त्रे ज्ञातव्यं». Śaṅkara treats the six words as the subject matter of a lesson whose content is assumed.

Śaṅkara takes bala as ‘a particular effort’ of articulation and sāman as pronouncing the sounds evenly, at a middle pace. Rāmānanda specifies bala as the inner and outer efforts of articulation (aspiration and the like). Madhva glosses the six words differently, as qualities (see the Dvaita position). The words themselves are technical terms whose exact scope the text does not define.
The base text, the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Śaṅkara’s mūla read śīkṣām with a long ī; Madhva’s text reads śikṣām (corrections.json). Śaṅkara explains the long vowel as Vedic. The meaning is the same.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose (brāhmaṇa style) in five short clauses: 8, 4, 4, 4 and 8 syllables. Not metrical.

beginner: Imagine a teacher who, before reading great poetry with a class, first makes sure everyone can pronounce it. That is what happens here. The Upaniṣad announces a lesson on pronunciation and lists six things to get right: each individual sound; the rise and fall of the voice; how long each vowel is held; the effort with which a sound is made; keeping an even pace; and how sounds join together when words run into each other. Then it says the lesson is complete. The details were taught elsewhere, by a teacher, out loud. The point the commentators draw is simple: a text whose purpose is understanding must first be received accurately, because a wrongly spoken word can carry a wrong meaning.
analogy: Like a music teacher who, before the first piece, names the basics — the notes, the pitch, the duration, the dynamics, the tempo, the phrasing — and says: everything else is built on these.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It announces an explanation of śikṣā, lists six items — varṇa, svara, mātrā, bala, sāman, santāna — and declares the lesson stated. It gives no definitions, no examples and no reason for placing the lesson here. All of that comes from the commentators.

commentary.q: Why does an Upaniṣad about meaning begin with pronunciation?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara’s first sentence answers it: because the Upaniṣad’s chief concern is the understanding of meaning, the lesson on pronunciation is begun so that care over the recitation of the text should not lapse — «अर्थज्ञानप्रधानत्वादुपनिषदः ग्रन्थपाठे यत्नोपरमो मा भूदिति शीक्षाध्याय आरभ्यते». The emphasis on meaning could tempt a student to neglect the sound; the lesson prevents that. Rāmānanda gives the same reason, «अर्थज्ञानस्यैव प्रधानत्वात्»: only a text correctly received can be correctly understood.

commentary.q: What is lost if the sound is wrong?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Kūranārāyaṇa and Rāmānanda both cite a verse they attribute to the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā: a mantra deficient in accent or letter does not convey its meaning — «मन्त्रो हीनस्स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह». (The verse is reported here as cited by them; this edition has not verified it in a text of the Śikṣā.) Kūranārāyaṇa also calls śikṣā the fifth limb of the Veda, recalled here as a means for studying the Upaniṣads: «शिक्षाख्यं पञ्चमं वेदाङ्गं त्रय्यन्ताध्ययनसाधनत्वेनाचक्ष्महे».

commentary.q: What do the six terms mean?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Śaṅkara glosses them briefly: varṇa is the sounds a and the rest, svara the accents udātta and the rest, mātrā the quantities short and the rest, bala a particular effort, sāman evenness of pronunciation at a middle pace, santāna continuity, that is saṃhitā — «सन्तानः सन्ततिः, संहितेत्यर्थः». Kūranārāyaṇa expands each from the śikṣā and prātiśākhya literature: mātrā is the measure of the time taken to utter a sound, «मात्रा उच्चारणक्रियाकालस्य इयत्ता»; svara covers the ‘four distinctions of sound produced by place of articulation’, udātta, anudātta, svarita and pracaya («स्थानविशेषनिबन्धनाः ध्वनिभेदाश्चत्वारः उदात्तानुदात्तस्वरितप्रचयाः»). Rāmānanda specifies bala as the inner and outer efforts of articulation, «बलम् बाह्याभ्यन्तरप्रयत्नरूपम्». The list moves from the smallest unit (the sound) through its properties (accent, length, effort) to the way sounds are delivered and joined.

commentary.q: Why is the lesson so short?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Kūranārāyaṇa says that because the particulars of the sounds and their fruit are not stated here, all of it is to be learned in the science of śikṣā; the passage only recalls it at the proper moment — «तस्य सर्वस्य प्रसङ्गादवसरे स्मरणमात्रं कृतमस्माभिरिति भावः». The anuvāka is a reminder, placed where a student of the Upaniṣad needs it, of a discipline learned from a teacher’s voice.

advaita.text: For Śaṅkara the lesson serves the Upaniṣad’s real purpose, knowledge of meaning, by protecting the text through which that knowledge comes: «अर्थज्ञानप्रधानत्वादुपनिषदः». He gives the six terms short technical glosses and draws no further doctrine from them.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa reads the anuvāka as recalling the śikṣā-śāstra so that faults of accent and letter are avoided, since a faulty Veda does not accomplish what is intended («स्वरवर्णादिदुष्टस्य वेदस्याभिमतासाधकत्वात्»). Rāmānanda agrees and adds that the lesson is needed before the text that follows («अध्येष्यमाणेऽग्रिमग्रन्थेऽयमावश्यकः»). Their reading of the anuvāka is practical and agrees with Śaṅkara’s.

dvaita.text: Madhva’s comment glosses each term by an etymology that turns it into a quality: varṇa is ‘the one to be chosen’ («वरणीयो वर्णः»), mātrā ‘the protector through measure’ («मानात् त्राता मात्रा»), and the last three are ‘having the form of strength’, ‘the same in all forms’ and ‘continuous’ («समश्च सर्वरूपेषु । सन्ततश्च»). The masculine forms point to a person; in keeping with his opening verse, which names the Brahman of the Upaniṣad as Viṣṇu (see 1.1), the subject is presumably the Lord. The short comment does not name him; that identification is an inference.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators read the anuvāka as a practical lesson on recitation. Madhva reads its six words as names of qualities, apparently of the Lord. Nothing in the comments of the first group attacks the second; the readings simply work at different levels.

parallels.quote: शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति
parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka lists śikṣā first among the six auxiliary sciences, and places all of them, with the four Vedas, under the ‘lower’ knowledge. The Taittirīya, by contrast, keeps the lesson on pronunciation inside an Upaniṣad, as a preparation for the higher.

contemporary.text: We copy and paste texts without ever hearing them, and errors spread with each copy. This anuvāka belongs to a culture that kept its texts for centuries by voice, and it begins its account of the highest knowledge with a checklist for accurate reception: the sound, the pitch, the length, the effort, the pace, the joins. Whatever the medium, the lesson holds — meaning depends on fidelity to the words, and fidelity is a skill that has to be taught. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Think of a word or a name you mispronounced for years. What changed when you learned it properly?
reflect.deeper: Why might a tradition that values meaning above all insist so strongly on the exact form of the words?
reflect.practice: Read one sentence aloud slowly, attending only to each sound and where it is made. Then read it again for its meaning, and notice whether the first reading changed the second.

references.text: Kūranārāyaṇa’s comment quotes extensively from the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā and the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya (with the editor’s references, e.g. ‘तै.प्रा. २३-२४’). These citations are reported as his; this edition has not checked them against those works.
Gopālānanda (a modern commentator in the six-commentary edition) gives the same reason as Śaṅkara: the lesson is heard first so that mistakes of accent do not occur in reading the Upaniṣad.

flags.note: The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha prefixes ॐ to the anuvāka, and Madhva’s text reads śikṣām for śīkṣām (corrections.json).
The Dvaita reading (the six terms as qualities of the Lord) is inferred from the masculine forms of Madhva’s short gloss and his opening verse; the gloss itself does not name its subject.
